nodes.title: Rank bounds from descent via 2-isogeny
nodes.statement: With the notation of two-isogeny-descent-map write n_i = 2^{e_i}, n_i′ = 2^{e_i′}. Then rank E(ℚ) = rank E′(ℚ) = e₁ + e₁′ − 2. Consequently, with ñ₁ = 2^{ẽ₁} ≤ n₁ the order of the subgroup generated by classes d₁ for which an explicit rational point on H(d₁, c, d/d₁) is exhibited (and the same with primes), ẽ₁ + ẽ₁′ − 2 ≤ rank E(ℚ) ≤ e₂ + e₂′ − 2, where n₂ and n₂′ are computed by quartic-local-solubility at the places dividing 2dd′ and ∞ (all other places are automatic). The lower bound is used only together with an upper bound certificate; rank = e₂ + e₂′ − 2 is certified when ñ₁ = n₂ and ñ₁′ = n₂′.
hypotheses: E, E′, α, α′ as in two-isogeny-descent-map.
proofSteps: φ′ ∘ φ = [2] gives the exact sequence 0 → E′(ℚ)[φ′]/φ(E(ℚ)[2]) → E′(ℚ)/φ(E(ℚ)) → E(ℚ)/2E(ℚ) → E(ℚ)/φ′(E′(ℚ)) → 0, so #E(ℚ)/2E(ℚ) = n₁n₁′/2 if d′ is not a square and n₁n₁′ if d′ is a square (Cremona p. 86).
#E(ℚ)/2E(ℚ) = 2^{rank} · #E(ℚ)[2] (Tau Ceti AddSubgroup.index_range_nsmul_of_fg with E(ℚ) finitely generated) and #E(ℚ)[2] = 2 or 4 according as d′ is a non-square or a square; so 2^{rank} = n₁n₁′/4.
α(E(ℚ)) ⊆ S^{(φ′)} gives n₁ ≤ n₂; exhibited points give subgroups of α(E(ℚ)).
Local solubility outside 2dd′ ∞ is automatic (quartic-local-solubility-correct; Aitken–Lemmermeyer Theorem 5).
acceptance: Cremona, Fermigier's curve c = 36861504658225, d = 1807580157674409809510400: n₁ = n₂ = 256 and n₁′ = n₂′ = 128, so the rank is 13 (fermigier-rank-thirteen).
For the five curves of rank-zero-curves, n₂n₂′ = 4, so the rank is 0.

nodes.title: Cremona's rational height difference bound
nodes.statement: For a nonsingular integral standard Weierstrass equation W over Q with discriminant Δ, j-invariant j and b₂, let 2*=1 if b₂=0 and 2 otherwise. Put μ_C=((log|Δ| + log⁺j)/6 + log⁺(b₂/12) + log(2*))/2, where log⁺t=log max(1,|t|), exactly as Cremona III Proposition 3.5.1 p.77. For every rational point P, in the PINNED Tau Ceti normalization, −h(j)/24−μ_C−961/1000 ≤ P.canonicalHeight−P.naiveHeight/2 ≤ μ_C+107/100. Cremona uses the doubled height and constants 1.922,2.14; divide the entire inequality and μ by two. Δ≠0 follows from IsElliptic; P=O has both heights zero. The number-field extension has now been independently checked in Silverman Theorem1.1, p.725, with its exact absolute height and archimedean weights recorded in suggestedOmissions; its Lean interface remains omitted.
hypotheses: W a nonsingular integral standard Weierstrass equation over Q, with all a_i integral and Δ≠0; P in W.toAffine.Point, including O.

Pinned Tau Ceti ĥ is half Cremona’s displayed height; the normalization is established by the actual limit definitions and Cremona footnote3. General K is a separately omitted weighted-height interface, with primary statement now verified.
proofSteps: Read the integral standard-equation over Q hypotheses of Proposition 3.5.1. Use log⁺t=log max(1,|t|), with (log|Δ|+log⁺j)/6 and log⁺(b₂/12) outside that quotient; distinguish log⁺j from the logarithmic height h(j).
Apply the proposition to 2·P.canonicalHeight and P.naiveHeight and divide by two. Use the pinned canonicalHeight rather than a fresh limiting function.

Choose an outward rational enclosure of μ_C+h(j)/24+961/1000 and μ_C+107/100 using CN.4; propagate through doubling enclosures. No rational result is generalized to a number field without its own source.
acceptance: On y²=x³+B for nonzero integral B, the constant reduces to μ_C=log|432B²|/12, and the lower/upper constants are μ_C+961/1000 and μ_C+107/100 because j=b₂=0.
Dividing the entire displayed Cremona inequality by two gives the pinned bound; O satisfies it with both heights zero.
Refines pinned Point.abs_canonicalHeight_sub_naiveHeight_le, whose bound is existential.

nodes.title: Certified enclosure of the canonical height by doubling
nodes.statement: For W over ℚ with integral coefficients, a point P ∈ E(ℚ) and n ∈ ℕ, canonicalHeightEnclosure W P n λ⁻ λ⁺ c⁻ c⁺ takes four explicit rational inputs and is a closed interval [ℓ, u] with rational endpoints containing ĥ(P) (Tau Ceti canonicalHeight), computed as follows: form Q = 2ⁿ·P exactly in Mathlib's group law over ℚ; if Q = O then ĥ(P) = 0 and the interval is [0,0]; otherwise H = max(|a|, b) for x(Q) = a/b in lowest terms and [λ⁻, λ⁺] ∋ log H is a certified rational enclosure; with nonnegative rational bounds c⁻ ≥ h(j)/24 + μ_C(W) + 961/1000 and c⁺ ≥ μ_C(W) + 107/100 (explicit-height-difference-bound, logs enclosed the same way), ℓ = (λ⁻/2 − c⁻)/4ⁿ and u = (λ⁺/2 + c⁺)/4ⁿ. The width is at most ((λ⁺ − λ⁻)/2 + c⁺ + c⁻)/4ⁿ, with equality when Q≠O. To obtain any requested width choose the CN.4 log enclosure to have uniformly bounded width (for example ≤1), choose fixed certified c⁻,c⁺, then increase n. No uniform decay is claimed for arbitrarily widening input log intervals. Pairings ⟨P, R⟩ = (ĥ(P + R) − ĥ(P) − ĥ(R))/2 are enclosed by interval arithmetic on three enclosures.
hypotheses: W over ℚ, integral, elliptic; P∈W.toAffine.Point; n∈ℕ.
Explicit rational λ⁻≤λ⁺, c⁻≥0, c⁺≥0. Containment requires λ⁻≤naiveHeight(2ⁿP)≤λ⁺ and c⁻≥h(j)/24+μ_C(W)+961/1000, c⁺≥μ_C(W)+107/100. The Q=O branch returns [0,0] without a logarithm evaluation.
CN.4 supplies certified logarithm/error endpoints at requested precision; this exact-arithmetic constructor does not claim that the supplier has been implemented.
proofSteps: ĥ(2ⁿP) = 4ⁿĥ(P) (Tau Ceti Point.canonicalHeight_nsmul), and explicit-height-difference-bound applied to Q = 2ⁿP gives h(Q)/2 − c⁻ ≤ ĥ(Q) ≤ h(Q)/2 + c⁺; divide by 4ⁿ.
h(Q) = log H by Mathlib Rat.mulHeight₁_eq_max and Tau Ceti Point.naiveHeight_eq_logHeight₁; interval arithmetic by CN.4 rational-interval-product.
Only exact rational arithmetic and the logarithm enclosures enter; no floating-point value is trusted.
acceptance: For y²=x³−2 and P=(3,5), certify at n=6 a log interval of width≤1 and nonnegative rational errors with (λ⁺−λ⁻)/2+c⁺+c⁻<40; the exact width is then <10⁻². This is a planned CN.4 producer regression, not a claimed executed approximation.
For a point of order 2^k the computation reaches Q = O for n ≥ k and returns [0,0]; for other torsion points the enclosures contain 0 and shrink to {0}.

nodes.title: Independence and regulator lower bound from certified heights
nodes.statement: Let P₁,…,P_r ∈ E(ℚ) and let I_{ij} be rational intervals with ⟨P_i, P_j⟩ ∈ I_{ij} (canonical-height-enclosure; ⟨·,·⟩ Tau Ceti's neronTatePairing, ⟨P,P⟩ = ĥ(P)). If the interval determinant of (I_{ij}) has positive lower endpoint δ > 0, then the images of P₁,…,P_r in E(ℚ)/E(ℚ)_tors are ℤ-linearly independent, rank E(ℚ) ≥ r, and det(⟨P_i, P_j⟩) ≥ δ. If moreover P₁,…,P_r is a basis of E(ℚ)/E(ℚ)_tors then Tau Ceti's regulator satisfies regulator ≥ δ.
hypotheses: W over ℚ elliptic with integral coefficients; enclosures from canonical-height-enclosure.
proofSteps: If Σ n_j P_j is torsion with n ≠ 0, then Σ_j ⟨P_i, P_j⟩ n_j = ⟨P_i, Σ_j n_j P_j⟩ = 0 for all i (bilinearity; Tau Ceti neronTatePairing_eq_zero_of_isOfFinAddOrder_right), so the Gram matrix is singular, contradicting det ≥ δ > 0.
The interval determinant encloses the true determinant (CN.4 interval arithmetic soundness), so det ≥ δ.

nodes.title: Lower bound for the canonical height of non-torsion points by a certified search
nodes.statement: Let W over ℚ be integral and elliptic, c⁻ a rational upper bound for h(j)/24 + μ_C(E) + 961/1000 (μ_C is cremonaMu, half of Cremona’s μ) (explicit-height-difference-bound), and B > 0. Let L be the finite set of P ∈ E(ℚ) with naiveHeight(P) ≤ B, enumerated completely (ED.0 bounded-height enumeration of x ∈ ℚ with h(x) ≤ B, followed by an exact test whether f(x) is a rational square). Put λ = min(B/2 − c⁻, min{ℓ_P : P ∈ L non-torsion}), where ℓ_P is the lower endpoint of a canonical-height-enclosure of P. If λ > 0, then ĥ(Q) ≥ λ for every non-torsion Q ∈ E(ℚ).

proofSteps: If naiveHeight(Q) > B then ĥ(Q) ≥ naiveHeight(Q)/2 − c⁻ > B/2 − c⁻ ≥ λ by the lower half of explicit-height-difference-bound.
Otherwise Q ∈ L, and Q non-torsion gives ĥ(Q) ≥ ℓ_Q ≥ λ.

nodes.title: Index bound from a height lower bound and Minkowski's theorem
nodes.statement: Let P₁,…,P_r ∈ E(ℚ) (r ≥ 1) be independent modulo torsion, L their span in E(ℚ)/E(ℚ)_tors, L̄ = {Q : nQ ∈ L for some n ≥ 1} its saturation and n = [L̄ : L]. Let λ > 0 with ĥ(Q) ≥ λ for every non-torsion Q ∈ E(ℚ) (height-lower-bound-by-search), and let γ_r be any constant such that every positive definite real quadratic form in r variables of determinant D takes a value ≤ γ_r·D^{1/r} at some nonzero integral vector; γ_r = (4/π)·Γ(r/2 + 1)^{2/r} is such a constant (Minkowski), and γ₁ = 1, γ₂ = (4/3)^{1/2} are the exact Hermite values. Then n ≤ R^{1/2}·(γ_r/λ)^{r/2}, where R = det(⟨P_i, P_j⟩) in Tau Ceti's normalisation. If rank E(ℚ) = r then L̄ = E(ℚ)/E(ℚ)_tors and n is the index of the subgroup generated by the P_i and the torsion.
hypotheses: P_i independent modulo torsion (e.g. by regulator-lower-bound); λ as stated; any of the listed γ_r.
proofSteps: L̄ is a lattice of rank r with Gram determinant R(L̄) = R/n² (index–covolume relation for the Gram determinant). This is the same Gram-lattice argument as Siksek equation(27), applied to the saturated rational span; that reduction, and the harmless weakening of >λ to ≥λ, are adaptations rather than extra generality printed in Theorem3.1.

Minkowski's convex-body theorem (Mathlib exists_ne_zero_mem_lattice_of_measure_mul_two_pow_le_measure) for the ellipsoid {x : ĥ(Σ x_i Q_i) ≤ t} in a basis Q_i of L̄, with InnerProductSpace.volume_ball, gives a nonzero Q ∈ L̄ with ĥ(Q) ≤ γ_r R(L̄)^{1/r}.
Q is non-torsion, so λ ≤ ĥ(Q) ≤ γ_r (R/n²)^{1/r}; solve for n.
acceptance: Rank2 exact numerical regression: R≤9, λ≥1 and γ₂²=4/3 give n²≤12, hence n≤3. This is an arithmetic bound with supplied certified inputs, independent of unavailable Prickett decimals.

nodes.title: p-saturated subgroups
nodes.statement: Let A be an abelian group, G ≤ A a subgroup and p a prime. G is p-saturated in A (IsPSaturated G p) if every a ∈ A with p·a ∈ G lies in G; G is saturated if it is p-saturated for every prime p. Equivalently: A[p] ≤ G and G ∩ pA = pG. If [A : G] is finite, G is p-saturated iff p ∤ [A : G]; G is saturated iff [A : G] = 1.
hypotheses: A an additive commutative group (A = E(ℚ) or J(ℚ) in the applications); G an AddSubgroup; p prime.
proofSteps: The equivalence: if G is p-saturated then A[p] ≤ G (p·t = 0 ∈ G) and pa ∈ G forces a ∈ G; conversely pa = g ∈ G ∩ pA = pG gives g = pg′, so a − g′ ∈ A[p] ≤ G.
Finite index: if p | [A:G], Cauchy's theorem in A/G gives a ∉ G with pa ∈ G; if p ∤ [A:G] and pa ∈ G, the class of a has order dividing p and [A:G], hence is trivial.
acceptance: In A = ℤ, G = 6ℤ is 5-saturated but neither 2- nor 3-saturated.
G = 0 in ℤ/pℤ is not p-saturated.

nodes.title: p-saturation from jointly injective reductions
nodes.statement: Let A be an abelian group, G ≤ A a subgroup with G/pG finite, p a prime, and ψ_i : A → C_i (i = 1,…,m) homomorphisms into abelian groups with pC_i = 0. If (a) the induced map G/pG → ∏_i C_i is injective and (b) A[p] ≤ G, then G is p-saturated in A. Standard choices: ψ_q : A → B_q → B_q/pB_q with B_q = Ẽ(𝔽_q) (resp. J̃(𝔽_q)) the reduction at a prime q of good reduction (EllipticCurves Layer 4; Jacobians by the RP.1 request), useful when p | #B_q; for p = 2 and A = E(ℚ), the descent map μ : E(ℚ) → M (kernel 2E(ℚ)) or its local components. Condition (b) is certified by the torsion certificate (torsion-by-reduction): it holds when A[p] = 0 or when generators of A[p] are among the generators of G.
hypotheses: A abelian; G ≤ A given by generators g₁,…,g_s, so G/pG is spanned by their classes; p prime; ψ_i homomorphisms with p-torsion targets.
proofSteps: Each ψ_i kills pA, hence G ∩ pA ≤ ker(G → ∏ C_i) = pG by (a); so G ∩ pA = pG.
With (b), p-saturated by the characterisation in p-saturated.

Practical form (Siksek §4.1): include free generators and a basis of the torsion modulo p; the p-divisible relation space V_p lies in every kernel of the finite reduction maps. If their joint kernel is zero, V_p=0. General p-primary reduction groups are handled by B_q/pB_q, not by assuming p²∤#B_q.
For p = 2 and μ: Tau Ceti ker_μ_eq gives ker μ = 2E(ℚ), so injectivity of G/2G → M is decided in the explicit square classes.

nodes.statement: Let A be a finitely generated abelian group, G ≤ A, ℓ a prime and ψ_i : A → C_i homomorphisms with ℓC_i = 0. nodes.title: Certified torsion subgroups
nodes.statement: (a) Let A be an abelian group and, for primes q₁,…,q_k, ρ_i : A → B_i homomorphisms into finite groups that are injective on torsion of order prime to q_i. Then for every prime ℓ, v_ℓ(#A_tors) ≤ min{v_ℓ(#B_i) : q_i ≠ ℓ}; if an explicit finite subgroup T₀ ≤ A_tors attains these bounds for all ℓ, then A_tors = T₀. (b) For E/ℚ in the model y² = x³ + ax² + bx + c (a = b₂, b = 8b₄, c = 16b₆, integral), every torsion point has x, y ∈ ℤ and y = 0 or y² | Δ₀ = 27c² + 4a³c + 4b³ − a²b² − 18abc; enumerating these candidates and computing orders gives E(ℚ)_tors exactly (Cremona's algorithm). Reduction at good odd q is injective on E(ℚ)_tors (EllipticCurves Layer 6); for Jacobians of curves over ℚ with good reduction at q, reduction is injective on torsion of order prime to q, and on all torsion for q ≥ 3 (requested from RP.1).
hypotheses: (a) A abelian, B_i finite, and for every prime ℓ there is at least one i with q_i ≠ ℓ; this makes each displayed minimum nonempty and bounds every primary torsion subgroup. (b) W over ℚ elliptic, coefficients integral.
proofSteps: (a) The ℓ-primary part of A_tors embeds into B_i whenever q_i ≠ ℓ (Subgroup.card_dvd_of_injective).

(b) Lutz–Nagell (Cremona Prop. 3.3.1) and Prop. 3.3.2: if 2P = O then y = 0; otherwise P and 2P are integral and the tangent slope is integral, so y | f′(x) and y² | Δ₀ by the displayed identity; orders by repeated addition until O or a non-integral point (at most 12 steps by Mazur).

nodes.title: Certified finite-index subgroup of a Mordell–Weil group
nodes.statement: Let A be a finitely generated abelian group (A = J(ℚ) for the Jacobian J of a smooth proper curve over ℚ with a rational point, finite generation from RP.1; or A = E(ℚ)) and Π a finite set of primes. A finite-index subgroup certificate (FiniteIndexSubgroupCertificate A Π) consists of: generators g₁,…,g_s ∈ A of G = ⟨g_i⟩; a natural number r with a certificate of rank A ≤ r (an algebraic descent bound: rank-upper-bound, two-isogeny-rank-bound or genus-two-descent-rank-bound) and a certificate of rank G ≥ r (regulator-lower-bound or reduction-rank-lower-bound); the torsion subgroup A_tors as an explicit finite list (torsion-by-reduction); and for each p ∈ Π a p-saturation certificate for G (saturation-certificate). Consequences: rank G = rank A = r, [A : G] is finite and coprime to every p ∈ Π. A rank upper bound that rests on an unproved hypothesis (for instance the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture) is not a field of the certificate: a theorem using it states the hypothesis rank A ≤ r explicitly.
hypotheses: A an additive commutative group with AddGroup.FG A; Π a finite set of primes.
proofSteps: Finite index: rank G = rank A for a subgroup of a finitely generated abelian group (Module.finrank ℤ) gives A/G finite.
Coprimality: p-saturated with finite index ⇔ p ∤ [A:G] (p-saturated).

nodes.title: Certified Mordell–Weil basis
nodes.statement: Let W over ℚ be elliptic with integral coefficients, T = E(ℚ)_tors certified (torsion-by-reduction), and P₁,…,P_r ∈ E(ℚ). Assume: (i) rank E(ℚ) ≤ r (rank-upper-bound or two-isogeny-rank-bound); (ii) det(⟨P_i, P_j⟩) ≥ δ > 0 (regulator-lower-bound); (iii) λ > 0 with ĥ ≥ λ on non-torsion points (height-lower-bound-by-search) and N = ⌊R⁺^{1/2}(γ_r/λ)^{r/2}⌋ with R⁺ an upper endpoint for det(⟨P_i,P_j⟩) (index-bound); (iv) G = ⟨T, P₁,…,P_r⟩ is p-saturated in E(ℚ) for every prime p ≤ N (saturation-certificate). Then E(ℚ) = G = T ⊕ ℤP₁ ⊕ … ⊕ ℤP_r, rank E(ℚ) = r and regulator(E) = det(⟨P_i, P_j⟩). The four inputs are each required: the conclusion combines an upper and a lower bound only when both certificates exist. For r=0, use the algebraic rank bound and complete torsion directly; the positive-dimensional index formula and γ_r are required only for r≥1.
hypotheses: As listed; T given as an explicit finite set of points.
proofSteps: (i) and (ii) give rank E(ℚ) = r and finite index of G (finite-index-subgroup-certificate).
[E(ℚ) : G] = [E(ℚ)/T : L] ≤ N by index-bound, since G ⊇ T.
A prime p dividing [E(ℚ):G] satisfies p ≤ N and contradicts p-saturation (p-saturated: finite index and p-saturated ⇒ p ∤ index); so the index is 1.
The regulator is |det| on a basis (Tau Ceti regulator_eq_abs_det_neronTateGramMatrix).
acceptance: y² = x³ − x: r = 0, T = E[2], G = T = E(ℚ) (index bound vacuous).
Cremona's rank-one strategy (§3.5) is the case r = 1: if λ > R⁺/4, with R⁺ ≥ ĥ(P₁) the upper endpoint used in (iii), then N = 1 and P₁ generates E(ℚ) modulo torsion.

nodes.title: Rank bound for genus-two Jacobians by the x − T descent
nodes.statement: Let C : y² = f(x) with f ∈ ℤ[x] separable of degree 6, C(ℚ) ≠ ∅, J its Jacobian, L = ℚ[T]/(f) and L_K = K[T]/(f) for K = ℚ or ℚ_v. (a) The map x − T sending the class of a good divisor Σ n_P P to Π (x_P − T)^{n_P} is a well-defined homomorphism J(K) → L_K^×/(L_K^{×2}K^×) with image in the kernel of the norm to K^×/K^{×2}; (b) for S ⊇ {2, ∞} ∪ {p | disc f}, the image of J(ℚ) lies in the subgroup H of classes unramified outside S with square norm, and in H′ = {h ∈ H : the image of h in L_p^×/(L_p^{×2}ℚ_p^×) lies in (x − T)(J(ℚ_p)) for all p ∈ S}; (c) [ker(x − T) : 2J(K)] = 1 if f has a root in K or the six roots admit a Gal(K^sep/K)-stable partition into two unordered triples, and 2 otherwise; (d) #J(ℚ_p)/2J(ℚ_p) = |2|_p^{-2}·#J(ℚ_p)[2]. Hence rank J(ℚ) ≤ dim_{𝔽₂} H′ + log₂[ker(x − T) : 2J(ℚ)] − dim_{𝔽₂} J(ℚ)[2].
hypotheses: C, J as stated; J(ℚ) finitely generated (RP.1 request); local images (x − T)(J(ℚ_p)) certified by the method of local-descent-image with the count (d).
proofSteps: (a) Flynn–Poonen–Schaefer Prop. 2 (linear equivalence changes the value by squares times constants; the norm is a square).
(b) Prop. 3 and diagram (6).
(c) Prop. 5: ker(x − T)/2J(K) is generated by [2P − ∞⁺ − ∞⁻]; it lies in 2J(K) iff one of its 16 halves is K-rational, which is the stated Galois condition.
(d) multiplication by 2 is n-to-1 on J(ℚ_p) and multiplies Haar measure by |2|_p^2 (Lemma 3); the Lie-group structure is the RP.1 request.
acceptance: C₀(5) (fps-genus-two-mordell-weil): H′ = 0 and [ker : 2J(ℚ)] = 2, so rank J(ℚ) ≤ 1.

nodes.title: The Lind–Reichardt curve: a nontrivial torsor class
nodes.statement: The genus-one curve C : 2z² = x⁴ − 17y⁴ (equivalently U² − 17W² = 2Z², UW = V², or v² = 2u⁴ − 34 with v = 2z/y², u = x/y) has points over ℝ and over every ℚ_p but no rational point. In the 2-isogeny descent for E : y² = x³ − 68x (c = 0, d = −68), C is the homogeneous space H(2, 0, −34); hence the class 2 ∈ ℚ^×/ℚ^{×2} lies in the φ′-Selmer group S^{(φ′)} but not in α(E(ℚ)). The quartic's invariants are I = 12·2·(−34) = −816 and J = 0, so its Jacobian is Y² = X³ + 22032X ≅ y² = x³ + 17x (22032 = 6⁴·17), the curve E′ : y² = x³ + 272x up to isomorphism; under the RP.1 identification of S^{(φ′)}/α(E(ℚ)) with Ш(E′/ℚ)[φ′], C is a nonzero element of Ш(E′/ℚ)[2].
hypotheses: Places: ∞, 2 and 17 are the only places where local solubility needs a computation (quartic-local-solubility-correct).
proofSteps: Local solubility: quarticLocallySoluble (2u⁴ − 34) v = true for v ∈ {2, 17, ∞} (certified run of quartic-local-solubility); Aitken–Lemmermeyer Theorem 4 with q = 17, d = 2 proves the same by conics.
No global point: Aitken–Lemmermeyer Lemma 6 — a nontrivial solution forces 2 to be a fourth power modulo 17, but the fourth powers modulo 17 are {1, 4, 13, 16}.

Descent reading: H(d₁, c, d/d₁) with d₁ = 2, c = 0, d = −68 is v² = 2u⁴ − 34 (two-isogeny-descent-map); everywhere local solubility puts 2 in S^{(φ′)}, the absence of rational points keeps it out of α(E(ℚ)).
Jacobian: Cremona (3.6.3), E_{I,J} : Y² = X³ − 27IX − 27J with I = 12ae − 3bd + c², J = 72ace + 9bcd − 27ad² − 27eb² − 2c³ for (a,b,c,d,e) = (2,0,0,0,−34).
acceptance: The curve passes the certified local tests at 2, 17 and ∞, and the φ′-Selmer computation for c = 0, d = −68 returns n₂ = 8 (all classes ±1, ±2, ±17, ±34), while α(E(ℚ)) omits 2.
The torsor class is labelled as an element of the explicit Selmer group; its Ш reading uses the cohomological identification requested from RP.1, not an assumption.

nodes.title: Descent via 2-isogeny on Fermigier's rank-13 curve
nodes.statement: For E : y² = x(x² + cx + d) with c = 36861504658225 and d = 1807580157674409809510400 = 2¹⁵·3⁴·5²·7²·17·23·29·41·103·113·127·809, and d′ = c² − 4d = 1351540205037645734822109025 = 5²·11²·17·23·29·41·113·127·449·1381·5003·21587: the certified local tests at the 17 primes dividing 2dd′ and at ∞ give n₂ = 256 and n₂′ = 128, so rank E(ℚ) ≤ 8 + 7 − 2 = 13 (certified upper bound). Cremona reports explicit rational points on 7 + 6 nontrivial homogeneous spaces, giving n₁ = 256, n₁′ = 128 and rank E(ℚ) = 13; the lower bound requires those points.
hypotheses: Upper bound: two-isogeny-rank-bound with quartic-local-solubility; lower bound: rational points on H(d₁, c, d/d₁) for 7 values d₁ and on H(d₁′, c′, d′/d₁′) for 6 values d₁′.
proofSteps: Factorisations of d and d′ (exact; checked by multiplication).
Run quarticLocallySoluble over the 8192 signed squarefree divisors of d and of d′ at the primes of 2dd′ and ∞; the counts are 256 and 128.
Cremona's group-structure bookkeeping (A₂ generated by found classes) reduces the searches to 7 + 6 spaces.
acceptance: The certified local tests give n₂ = 256 and n₂′ = 128, hence rank E(ℚ) ≤ 13.
The equality rank = 13 is stated only with the 13 explicit points supplied (gap recorded).

sources.match: Exponents flattened by extraction (2¹⁵·3⁴·5²·7²).

sources.excerpt: Working with the isogenous curve, we obtain n01 = n02 = 128 after only searching six homogeneous spaces for points. Thus e1 = 8, e01 = 7 and the rank is 13.
sources.match: n₁′ = n₂′ = 128; the upper-bound half is certified by quartic-local-solubility, a transcription of Cremona's pseudocode.

nodes.title: Rank-zero elliptic curves of small conductor, with their rational points
nodes.statement: Each of the following curves has E(ℚ) finite, equal to the listed points: E15 : y² + xy + y = x³ + x², E(ℚ) = {O, (0,0), (−1,0), (0,−1)} ≅ ℤ/4; E17 : y² + xy + y = x³ − x² − x, {O, (0,0), (1,−1), (0,−1)} ≅ ℤ/4; E24 : y² = x³ − x² + x, {O, (0,0), (1,1), (1,−1)} ≅ ℤ/4; E40 : y² = x³ − 2x + 1, {O, (0,±1), (1,0)} ≅ ℤ/4; Morton's Y² = 4X³ − 11X² + 8X, {∞, (0,0), (1,±1), (2,±2)} ≅ ℤ/6. What is certified and how: rank 0 by two-isogeny-rank-bound with n₂n₂′ = 4 — in the shape y² = x(x² + cx + d) the data are (c, d) = (−7, 16), (9, 16), (−1, 1), (3, 1), (−11, 32) with (n₂, n₂′) = (1,4), (2,2), (1,4), (2,2), (2,2) — and the torsion subgroup by torsion-by-reduction (b), which finds exactly the listed points. For E11 : y² + y = x³ − x² the torsion subgroup {O, (0,0), (0,−1), (1,0), (1,−1)} ≅ ℤ/5 is certified, but its rank 0 is not (no rational 2-torsion, so a full 2-descent over the cubic field of x³ − 4x² + 16 is needed; gap).
hypotheses: Models: E15, E17 via s₂ = a₁² + 4a₂, s₄ = 8(a₁a₃ + 2a₄), s₆ = 16(a₃² + 4a₆) and the integral root x₀ (−4, resp. 4) of x³ + s₂x² + s₄x + s₆ (Cremona's pseudocode); E24 directly; E40 after x ↦ x + 1; Morton's curve via x = 4X, y = 4Y.
proofSteps: For each curve, two-isogeny-rank-bound with the certified local tests at the primes of 2dd′ ({2,3,5}, {2,17}, {2,3}, {2,5}, {2,7}) and ∞ gives rank ≤ e₂ + e₂′ − 2 = 0.
Torsion: Cremona's algorithm on y² = x³ + b₂x² + 8b₄x + 16b₆ lists the integral points with y = 0 or y² | Δ₀ and their orders; the result has 4, 4, 4, 4, 6 elements, matching the lists.
Transport of the lists back to the given models by the explicit coordinate changes.
acceptance: The certified data answer the ArithmeticDynamics request for E15, E17, E24, E40 and Morton's curve; E11's rank and the three genus-two curves are recorded as gaps.
Poonen prints E24(ℚ) with (−1, 1), which is not on the curve; the corrected list (1, −1) is used (recorded as ArithmeticDynamics/E402).

nodes.title: Mordell–Weil group of the Jacobian of C₀(5) (Flynn–Poonen–Schaefer)
nodes.statement: For C₀(5) : y² = x⁶ + 8x⁵ + 22x⁴ + 22x³ + 5x² + 6x + 1 with Jacobian J: J(ℚ) ≅ ℤ, and D = [∞⁺ − ∞⁻] generates a subgroup of index prime to 3. As a finite-index-subgroup-certificate with Π = {3}: generators {D}; r = 1; J(ℚ)_tors = 0; ⟨D⟩ 3-saturated. Certified ingredients: (i) torsion: #J(𝔽₃) = 9, #J(𝔽₅) = 41; (ii) rank ≤ 1: genus-two-descent-rank-bound with S = {2, 3701, ∞}, L of class number 1 with units u₁, u₂, u₃ (CN.2 certificate), H spanned by u₁ and u₃β₁β₂, local images at 2 and 3701 generated by [(2, √881) − ∞⁻] and [(−4, √185) − ∞⁻], H′ = 0, and [ker(x − T) : 2J(ℚ)] = 2 because the Galois group of f is S₆; (iii) rank ≥ 1: D ≠ 0 and J(ℚ)_tors = 0; (iv) 3-saturation: J(𝔽₃) ≅ ℤ/9 is generated by D̃, so D̃ ∉ 3J(𝔽₃).
hypotheses: J(ℚ) finitely generated (RP.1 request); reduction at 3 and 5 (RP.1 request).
proofSteps: (i) torsion-by-reduction (a) with q = 3, 5.
(ii) Lemmas 1–5 and Theorem 3 of Flynn–Poonen–Schaefer, each step an instance of genus-two-descent-rank-bound; f(2) = 881 ≡ 1 mod 8 and (185/3701) = 1 certify the local points.
(iii)–(iv) saturation-certificate with the single map J(ℚ) → J(𝔽₃)/3J(𝔽₃).
The number-field data (class number, units, factorisations of 2 and 3701) were verified unconditionally per the source; in the certificate they are CN.2 class-and-unit certificates.
acceptance: Answers part (a) of the ArithmeticDynamics request: J(ℚ) ≅ ℤ with ⟨D⟩ of index prime to 3, which is what the 3-adic Chabauty argument (ED.4) uses; whether D generates J(ℚ) is not decided by the source.

nodes.title: The subgroup of known points on X₀^dyn(6), with the conditional rank input labelled
nodes.statement: Let C = X₀^dyn(6) (genus 4, model G(u,w) = 0 in ℙ¹ × ℙ¹) with Jacobian J and ten known rational points P₀,…,P₉. Certified (algebraic): J(ℚ)_tors = 0 (#J(𝔽₇) = 2·7·11·47, #J(𝔽₁₃) = 3·17·23·43), and the subgroup G generated by the classes of degree-0 divisors supported on P₀,…,P₉ is ≅ ℤ³ (lower bound: reduction-rank-lower-bound with ℓ = 3 and S = {3,5,7,11,13}; upper bound: six explicit linear equivalences). Conditional (analytic, labelled separately): if L(J, s) extends to an entire function with the standard functional equation, the weak Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture holds for J, and L‴(J,1) ≠ 0 is certified, then rank J(ℚ) ≤ 3. Stoll reports L‴(C,1) ≈ 0.83601 numerically and L,L′,L″ vanishing to working precision; these approximations alone are not a proof of the additional nonvanishing hypothesis. Under the hypothesis rank J(ℚ) = 3, G has finite index and J(ℚ) is the saturation Ḡ of G; Stoll's Chabauty step uses Ḡ directly, so no p-saturation certificate is needed or provided by the source.
hypotheses: Hypothesis for the conditional part, stated explicitly and never as a certificate field: rank J(ℚ) ≤ 3.

An analytic derivation of rank≤3 additionally requires a certified L‴(J,1)≠0, hence analytic order≤3; numerical vanishing of lower derivatives is not needed for this upper bound and is not certified here.
proofSteps: Torsion: torsion-by-reduction (a) with q = 7, 13.
rank G ≥ 3: the degree-0 part of ⊕ℤP_i surjects onto (ℤ/3)³ in ∏_{q ∈ S} Pic(C/𝔽_q); rank G ≤ 3: the six relations (e.g. P₀ + P₆ + P₈ ∼ P₁ + P₇ + P₉), each certified by an explicit rational function.
Conditional rank: Stoll §4 and Theorem 7; the numerical L-value is not a certified enclosure and the hypotheses are open, so this input never enters a FiniteIndexSubgroupCertificate.
acceptance: Answers the ArithmeticDynamics request on X₀^dyn(6) with the exact split: G ≅ ℤ³ certified; finite index and J(ℚ) = Ḡ only under rank J(ℚ) = 3.
Acceptance of the stage: conditional analytic-rank input is labelled separately from algebraic rank certification.

nodes.title: Good-reduction Chabauty datum: curve, base point, smooth model and residue discs
nodes.statement: A good-reduction Chabauty datum (X, O, p, 𝒳) consists of a smooth projective geometrically integral curve X over ℚ of genus g ≥ 1, given by explicit equations; a rational point O ∈ X(ℚ); a prime p; and a smooth projective curve 𝒳 → Spec ℤ_p with geometrically connected fibres together with an isomorphism 𝒳_{ℚ_p} ≅ X_{ℚ_p}. Derived data, fixed by the definition: (i) the special fibre X̃ := 𝒳_{𝔽_p}, a smooth projective geometrically integral curve of genus g over 𝔽_p, and X̃(𝔽_p) its finite set of rational points; (ii) the reduction map red : X(ℚ_p) = 𝒳(ℤ_p) → X̃(𝔽_p) (the equality by the valuative criterion of properness), surjective by Hensel's lemma; (iii) for x̃ ∈ X̃(𝔽_p) the residue disc D(x̃) := red⁻¹(x̃) ⊆ X(ℚ_p), and a local parameter t_x̃, a function regular on a Zariski neighbourhood of x̃ in 𝒳 whose restriction to X̃ is a uniformiser at x̃; t_x̃ maps D(x̃) bijectively onto pℤ_p and, for every finite extension K/ℚ_p, the points of 𝒳(O_K) reducing to x̃ bijectively onto the maximal ideal m_K, the coordinates of the inverse being power series with ℤ_p-coefficients; (iv) the Jacobian J of X with the Abel–Jacobi embedding ι_O : X → J, P ↦ [P − O]; (v) the relative Jacobian 𝒥 := Pic⁰_{𝒳/ℤ_p}, an abelian scheme with 𝒥_{ℚ_p} ≅ J_{ℚ_p} and special fibre J̃ = Jac(X̃), and the reduction map red_J : J(ℚ_p) = 𝒥(ℤ_p) → J̃(𝔽_p) with red_J ∘ ι_O = ι_Õ ∘ red; its kernel is J¹(ℚ_p); (vi) the good-reduction pair (𝒳, Ō) of ColemanIntegration, Ō the closure of O, a section of 𝒳 → Spec ℤ_p and hence finite étale of degree one. The same definition is made over the ring of integers O_v of a completion K_v of a number field K at a finite place v, with 𝔽_p replaced by the residue field k_v and pℤ_p by the maximal ideal of O_v.
hypotheses: X smooth, projective, geometrically integral over ℚ (or over a number field K), genus g ≥ 1; O ∈ X(ℚ).
𝒳 smooth and projective over ℤ_p (resp. O_v) with generic fibre identified with X_{ℚ_p} (resp. X_{K_v}); this is the meaning of 'p is a prime of good reduction' throughout ED.4.
Points of X̃ are taken over 𝔽_p unless a finite extension is named; residue discs of non-rational points of X̃ contain no ℚ_p-points.
proofSteps: Reduction: X is proper, so X(ℚ_p) = 𝒳(ℤ_p) and each point reduces to a point of X̃(𝔽_p); smoothness of 𝒳 and Hensel's lemma make red surjective (McCallum–Poonen §5.2(1)).

Residue discs: a local parameter t_x̃ restricts to a formal coordinate of the completed local ring of 𝒳 at x̃, ℤ_p[[t]] after completion, so points of D(x̃) correspond to t ∈ pℤ_p (Siksek Lemma 3.1(iii)); this is the ℚ_p-point version of ColemanIntegration:L1/residue-disc-parametrisation for the pair (𝒳, Ō).

Jacobian model: 𝒥 = Pic⁰_{𝒳/ℤ_p} is an abelian scheme of relative dimension g (JacobianChallengePartII:JC1/relative-jacobian) whose fibres are the Jacobians of the fibres (JC1/jacobian-base-change); the section Ō gives the Abel–Jacobi morphism 𝒳 → 𝒥 extending ι_O, which yields red_J ∘ ι_O = ι_Õ ∘ red.
The section Ō is finite étale of degree one over ℤ_p, so (𝒳, Ō) satisfies the hypotheses of ColemanIntegration:L1/good-reduction-pair.
acceptance: For C₀(5) at p = 3 the residue discs are the four listed in datum_C05_three, and each of the six rational points lies in exactly one of them.
Degenerate case ℙ¹_{ℤ_p}: p + 1 discs, each parametrised by x − a or 1/x.

nodes.title: The p-adic abelian logarithm and the integration pairing
nodes.statement: Let K be a finite extension of ℚ_p with ring of integers O_K, residue field k and ramification index e, and A an abelian variety of dimension g over K. Write Lie(A) for its tangent space at 0 (a K-vector space of dimension g) and Ω_A := H⁰(A, Ω¹) for its space of regular 1-forms, which are the translation-invariant forms; evaluation at 0 identifies Ω_A with the dual Module.Dual K Lie(A). The abelian logarithm log_A : A(K) → Lie(A) is the unique group homomorphism that agrees with the formal logarithm on some open subgroup, constructed as follows. Let 𝒜 be the Néron model of A over O_K (an abelian scheme when A has good reduction), F̂ its formal group, the completion of 𝒜 along the zero section, a g-dimensional commutative formal Lie group over O_K once formal parameters s = (s₁, …, s_g) are chosen, and A¹(K) := ker(𝒜(O_K) → 𝒜(k)) = F̂(m_K). Let log_F̂ ∈ (K[[s]])^g be the formal logarithm, the unique homomorphism of formal groups F̂ → Ĝ_a^g over K whose linear term is the identity; its coordinates are the formal primitives of a basis of invariant differentials and converge on m_K^g. Put N := #𝒜(k) = [A(K) : A¹(K)] and log_A(x) := N⁻¹ log_F̂(s(N x)), identifying K^g with Lie(A) by ds at 0. The integration pairing is ⟨x, ω⟩ := ω(log_A x) ∈ K for x ∈ A(K), ω ∈ Ω_A. Properties: (a) log_A is a homomorphism, independent of the choices of formal parameters and of N among multiples of the exponent of 𝒜(k); (b) ker log_A = A(K)_tors, which is finite; (c) log_A is continuous, its differential at 0 is the identity, and for n > e/(p − 1) it maps the subgroup F̂(m_K^n) isomorphically onto the lattice (m_K^n)^g; (d) for a homomorphism φ : A → B of abelian varieties over K, log_B ∘ φ = dφ ∘ log_A, i.e. ⟨φ(x), ω⟩ = ⟨x, φ*ω⟩; for a finite extension K'/K, log_{A_{K'}} restricts to log_A on A(K); (e) the pairing A(K) × Ω_A → K is ℤ-bilinear and K-linear in ω, its kernel in Ω_A, {ω : ⟨x, ω⟩ = 0 ∀x}, is 0 and its kernel in A(K) is A(K)_tors; for each ω, x ↦ ⟨x, ω⟩ is the unique locally analytic homomorphism A(K) → K whose differential at 0 is ω. The compatible logarithms over finite K'/K first define log_A on A(ℚ̄_p). Over ℂ_p use the analytic logarithm of the ℂ_p-Lie group, extending this map continuously; the union over finite extensions alone does not define it on all A(ℂ_p) (KRZB Definition 3.8 and Proposition 3.16).
hypotheses: K finite over ℚ_p; A an abelian variety over K. Good reduction is not assumed; when A has good reduction 𝒜 is the abelian scheme extending A and 𝒜(k) is the group of points of its special fibre.
Normalisation: Lie(A) = T₀A and the pairing is evaluation of an invariant differential on a tangent vector; no sign or scaling is inserted.
proofSteps: Formal group: 𝒜 is smooth over O_K, so its completion along the zero section is Spf O_K[[s₁, …, s_g]] with a commutative formal group law (FiniteFlatGroupsAndIntegralPadicHodgeTheory:R07.1/formal-lie-group), and A(K) = 𝒜(O_K) by the Néron mapping property; 𝒜(O_K) → 𝒜(k) is surjective by smoothness, so A¹(K) has finite index N.

Formal logarithm: the invariant differentials of F̂ have O_K-integral coefficients and linear term ds_i; their formal primitives (ColemanIntegration:L0/formal-primitive) define log_F̂, a homomorphism to Ĝ_a^g because its differential is invariant; denominators of degree-n coefficients divide n, so log_F̂ converges on m_K^g (ColemanIntegration:L0/ultrametric-natcast-bound, L0/formal-primitive-radius).

Extension: A(K)/A¹(K) is finite of order N and Lie(A) is uniquely divisible, so x ↦ N⁻¹ log_F̂(s(N x)) is the unique homomorphism extending log_F̂|A¹(K); a change of parameters composes F̂ with a formal isomorphism, which log_F̂ absorbs (McCallum–Poonen §4.1 and Remark 4.1).

Kernel and local isomorphism: for n > e/(p − 1) the formal exponential converges on (m_K^n)^g and inverts log_F̂ there, so F̂(m_K^n) is torsion-free and ker log_A consists of elements with a multiple in a torsion-free group mapping to 0, i.e. A(K)_tors; A(K) is compact, so A(K)_tors is finite.

Functoriality: φ extends to the Néron models and induces a homomorphism of formal groups whose linear term is dφ; log_B ∘ φ̂ = dφ ∘ log_A by uniqueness of the formal logarithm (Katz–Rabinoff–Zureick-Brown §3.3).

Pairing: trivial kernel in Ω_A for the displayed order A(K) × Ω_A because log_A(A(K)) contains a lattice spanning Lie(A); uniqueness of the locally analytic homomorphism because the difference of two has zero differential, so it vanishes on an open subgroup of finite index and takes values in a torsion-free group.
acceptance: For the Jacobian of C₀(5) over ℚ_3, D' = 9·[∞⁺ − ∞⁻] lies in J¹(ℚ_3) and its logarithm in Flynn's parameters is ≡ (36, 3) (mod 3⁴) (Flynn–Poonen–Schaefer p.22).
For an elliptic curve with good reduction the construction is the formal logarithm on E¹(ℚ_p) extended by division by #Ẽ(𝔽_p).

nodes.title: Abelian integrals of regular differentials on a curve
nodes.statement: Let K be a finite extension of ℚ_p, X a smooth projective geometrically integral curve of genus g ≥ 1 over K and J its Jacobian. For any O ∈ X(K) the pullback ι_O* : H⁰(J, Ω¹) → H⁰(X, Ω¹) along ι_O(P) = [P − O] is an isomorphism of K-vector spaces that does not depend on O; for ω ∈ H⁰(X, Ω¹) write ω_J for the invariant form with ι_O*ω_J = ω. For a degree-zero divisor D = Σ n_i P_i on X_K̄ that is Gal(K̄/K)-stable, define ∫_D ω := ⟨[D], ω_J⟩ (pairing of ED.4/abelian-logarithm on J(K)), and for Q, Q' ∈ X(K) put ∫_Q^{Q'} ω := ∫_{Q' − Q} ω = ⟨ι_O(Q') − ι_O(Q), ω_J⟩. The continuous analytic abelian logarithm over ℂ_p defines the same formulas on X(ℂ_p); finite-extension formulas give only its restriction to algebraic points. Properties: (i) K-linear in ω and additive in D; ∫_Q^{Q'} + ∫_{Q'}^{Q''} = ∫_Q^{Q''}; (ii) ∫_D ω = 0 whenever [D] is torsion in J(K), in particular when D is principal, and conversely if ∫_D ω = 0 for all ω then [D] is torsion; (iii) η_{ω,O}(P) := ∫_O^P ω = ⟨ι_O(P), ω_J⟩, and changing O adds a constant; (iv) change of variables: for a nonconstant morphism ρ : X → Y of such curves over K and ω ∈ H⁰(Y, Ω¹), ∫_D ρ*ω = ∫_{ρ_*D} ω; (v) trace: for ρ finite and E a degree-zero divisor on Y, ∫_{ρ*E} ω = ∫_E Tr_ρ ω, where Tr_ρ : H⁰(X, Ω¹) → H⁰(Y, Ω¹) is the trace; (vi) base change: ∫ is compatible with finite extensions K'/K.
hypotheses: K finite over ℚ_p; X smooth projective geometrically integral of genus g ≥ 1 over K.
The definition uses only the abelian logarithm of J; no reduction hypothesis is made. When X has good reduction this integral equals the Coleman integral (ED.4/coleman-abelian-comparison).
proofSteps: The isomorphism ι_O* and its independence of O: two Abel–Jacobi maps differ by a translation and invariant forms are translation invariant (McCallum–Poonen §5.1 citing Milne; Siksek §3.3); requested from SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.3 together with the Jacobian (JacobianChallenge layers D–F).
(i)–(iii) follow from the corresponding properties of the pairing in ED.4/abelian-logarithm (homomorphism, torsion kernel, left non-degeneracy).

(iv) ρ induces ρ_* : J_X → J_Y with ρ_* ∘ ι_O = ι_{ρ(O)} ∘ ρ; functoriality of log (ED.4/abelian-logarithm (d)) gives ⟨ρ_*x, ω_J⟩ = ⟨x, (ρ_*)*ω_J⟩ and (ρ_*)*ω_J corresponds to ρ*ω (Siksek §3.1 change of variables).
(v) ρ* : J_Y → J_X on Picard groups pulls invariant forms back to the forms corresponding to traces; apply (d) of ED.4/abelian-logarithm to ρ*.
(vi) is ED.4/abelian-logarithm (d) for K'/K.
acceptance: McCallum–Poonen Example 3: ∫_{(0,1)}^{(−3,1)} dx/y ≡ 2·3 + 3⁴ and ∫_{(0,1)}^{(−3,1)} x dx/y ≡ 2·3² + 2·3³ (mod 3⁵) on C₀(5).
Degenerate case: ∫_Q^Q ω = 0.

suggestedOmissions.requiredSignature: Let K be a finite extension of ℚ_p, X a smooth projective geometrically integral curve of genus g ≥ 1 over K and J its Jacobian. For any O ∈ X(K) the pullback ι_O* : H⁰(J, Ω¹) → H⁰(X, Ω¹) along ι_O(P) = [P − O] is an isomorphism of K-vector spaces that does not depend on O; for ω ∈ H⁰(X, Ω¹) write ω_J for the invariant form with ι_O*ω_J = ω. For a degree-zero divisor D = Σ n_i P_i on X_K̄ that is Gal(K̄/K)-stable, define ∫_D ω := ⟨[D], ω_J⟩ (pairing of ED.4/abelian-logarithm on J(K)), and for Q, Q' ∈ X(K) put ∫_Q^{Q'} ω := ∫_{Q' − Q} ω = ⟨ι_O(Q') − ι_O(Q), ω_J⟩. The continuous analytic abelian logarithm over ℂ_p defines the same formulas on X(ℂ_p); finite-extension formulas give only its restriction to algebraic points. Properties: (i) K-linear in ω and additive in D; ∫_Q^{Q'} + ∫_{Q'}^{Q''} = ∫_Q^{Q''}; (ii) ∫_D ω = 0 whenever [D] is torsion in J(K), in particular when D is principal, and conversely if ∫_D ω = 0 for all ω then [D] is torsion; (iii) η_{ω,O}(P) := ∫_O^P ω = ⟨ι_O(P), ω_J⟩, and changing O adds a constant; (iv) change of variables: for a nonconstant morphism ρ : X → Y of such curves over K and ω ∈ H⁰(Y, Ω¹), ∫_D ρ*ω = ∫_{ρ_*D} ω; (v) trace: for ρ finite and E a degree-zero divisor on Y, ∫_{ρ*E} ω = ∫_E Tr_ρ ω, where Tr_ρ : H⁰(X, Ω¹) → H⁰(Y, Ω¹) is the trace; (vi) base change: ∫ is compatible with finite extensions K'/K. Hypotheses: K finite over ℚ_p; X smooth projective geometrically integral of genus g ≥ 1 over K. The definition uses only the abelian logarithm of J; no reduction hypothesis is made. When X has good reduction this integral equals the Coleman integral (ED.4/coleman-abelian-comparison). nodes.title: Tiny integrals: abelian integrals on a residue disc are power-series primitives
nodes.statement: Let (X, O, p, 𝒳) be a good-reduction Chabauty datum, K a finite extension of ℚ_p, x̃ ∈ X̃(𝔽_p) and t = t_x̃ a local parameter at x̃. Let ω ∈ H⁰(𝒳, Ω¹_{𝒳/ℤ_p}) be an integral regular differential. Then (a) in the completed local ring of 𝒳 at x̃, ω = w(t) dt with w ∈ ℤ_p[[t]], and the reduction ω̃ ∈ H⁰(X̃, Ω¹) has expansion w̃(t) dt at x̃ with w̃ = w mod p; (b) for all points Q, Q' of 𝒳(O_K) reducing to x̃, ∫_Q^{Q'} ω = I(t(Q')) − I(t(Q)) where I := PowerSeries.primitive w ∈ ℚ_p[[t]] (constant term 0), which converges on the open unit disc; (c) for fixed Q in the disc, P ↦ ∫_Q^P ω is the unique function on the disc given by a power series in t − t(Q) convergent on the open unit disc, with derivative w(t) and value 0 at Q; (d) if p is odd and K/ℚ_p is unramified and t(Q) = 0, then ∫_Q^P ω = α z + β z² with z = t(P), α = w(0) ∈ ℤ_p and β ∈ O_K. For a general ω ∈ H⁰(X_{ℚ_p}, Ω¹), apply (a)–(c) to p^k ω for k with p^k ω integral.
hypotheses: (X, O, p, 𝒳) a good-reduction Chabauty datum; ω integral (an element of H⁰(𝒳, Ω¹), a free ℤ_p-module of rank g whose reduction is H⁰(X̃, Ω¹)).
Points over a finite extension K are allowed; t(Q), t(Q') lie in the maximal ideal of O_K.
proofSteps: Q and Q' have the same reduction, so ι_O(Q') − ι_O(Q) lies in the kernel of reduction of 𝒥 (ED.4/good-reduction-chabauty-datum), where log_J is the formal logarithm (ED.4/abelian-logarithm).

With Q fixed, P ↦ [P − Q] is a morphism from the formal neighbourhood Spf O_K[[t − t(Q)]] of the disc to the formal group of 𝒥, so the formal parameters of [P − Q] are power series in t − t(Q) with O_K-coefficients and no constant term; composing with log_F̂ gives a power series convergent on the open disc (ColemanIntegration:L0/formal-primitive-radius) whose differential is the pullback of ω_J along P ↦ [P − Q], namely ω, because ω_J is translation invariant.

A power series convergent on the open disc is determined by its derivative and its value at one point (ColemanIntegration:L0/disc-primitive-unique, L0/formal-primitive-unique); comparing with primitive(w) gives (b) and (c).
(a) is the definition of integral differentials and their reduction in local coordinates (McCallum–Poonen §5.2(2)).
(d) The coefficient of z^{j+1} is w_j/(j + 1) and ord(z) ≥ 1; ord_p(j + 2) ≤ j for all j ≥ 0 when p is odd, so β = Σ_j w_{j+1} z^j/(j + 2) is integral (Siksek Lemma 3.2).
acceptance: McCallum–Poonen Example 3 (author copy p.11): on the disc of (0, 1) of y² = x⁶ + 8x⁵ + 22x⁴ + 22x³ + 5x² + 6x + 1 with t = x, ∫_{(0,1)}^{(−3,1)} dx/y = Σ a_i (−3)^{i+1}/(i + 1) where (1 + 6x + …)^{−1/2} = Σ a_i x^i = 1 − 3x + 11x² − 56x³ + ⋯, giving ≡ 2·3 + 3⁴ (mod 3⁵).
Degenerate case: for Q' = Q both sides vanish.

nodes.title: Pairing a point of the kernel of reduction with a differential by tiny integrals
nodes.statement: Let (X, O, p, 𝒳) be a good-reduction Chabauty datum of genus g, and P' ∈ X(ℚ_p) whose reduction x̃' satisfies dim H⁰(X̃, O(g·x̃')) = 1 (x̃' is not a Weierstrass point of X̃). Then every D ∈ J¹(ℚ_p) = ker(red_J) is uniquely represented as D = [Q₁ + ⋯ + Q_g − g·P'] with Q₁ + ⋯ + Q_g an effective divisor defined over ℚ_p (a Galois-stable geometric multiset, allowing repeated points) whose points Q_j ∈ X(ℚ̄_p) all reduce to x̃'. Independently of the Weierstrass hypothesis, whenever D = [Q₁ + ⋯ + Q_g − g·P'] with all Q_j in the residue disc of x̃', and ω ∈ H⁰(X_{ℚ_p}, Ω¹) has expansion w(t) dt at x̃' in a parameter t with t(P') = 0, and λ := primitive(w) = Σ_{n ≥ 1} λ_n t^n, then ⟨D, ω_J⟩ = Σ_j λ(t(Q_j)) = Σ_{n ≥ 1} λ_n s_n, where s_n = Σ_j t(Q_j)^n ∈ ℚ_p are the power sums of the roots of ∏_j (T − t(Q_j)) ∈ ℚ_p[T], computed from its coefficients by Newton's identities. In particular ⟨D, ω_J⟩ is computable to any p-adic precision from an effective representative of D + g·P'. Equivalently write E=Σ_x m_x[x] over closed points of X_{ℚ_p}: Σ_x m_x[κ(x):ℚ_p]=g and the value is Σ_x m_x Tr_{κ(x)/ℚ_p}(λ(t(x))). The representative is unique as an effective divisor, not as an ordering of geometric points. The characteristic polynomial and trace include every multiplicity.
hypotheses: Good-reduction datum; x̃' not a Weierstrass point of X̃ (h⁰(g x̃') = 1).
For g = 1 every point qualifies and the statement is the formal-group description of E¹.
proofSteps: Riemann–Roch on X gives an effective E of degree g with E ∼ D + g P'; reduction of divisors through the smooth model 𝒳 preserves linear equivalence, so Ẽ ∼ g x̃' on X̃ because D reduces to 0 (requested from SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.3).
h⁰(X̃, O(g x̃')) = 1 forces Ẽ = g x̃', so every point of E lies in the residue disc of x̃'; upper semicontinuity of h⁰ in the family 𝒳 gives h⁰(X, O(D + gP')) ≤ 1, hence uniqueness of E.
⟨D, ω_J⟩ = Σ_j ∫_{P'}^{Q_j} ω by ED.4/abelian-integral (i) over the field of definition of the Q_j, and each term is λ(t(Q_j)) by ED.4/tiny-integral-expansion (b) applied over that finite extension.

Work in one finite extension containing every support point of E, with compatible abelian logarithms. Finite summation commutes with the convergent primitive series; Galois equivariance groups conjugate terms into field traces. Newton identities compute the weighted power sums of the degree-g characteristic polynomial over ℚ_p (Stoll2008 Lemma5, pp.9–10). Uniqueness is the stated Riemann–Roch/specialisation argument, not asserted in that source passage.
acceptance: Stoll's evaluation on X₀^dyn(6) at p = 5 with P' = P₁ = (u, w) = (0, −1) and parameter u: Stoll exhibits effective degree-four D_j' supported in the disc of P₁ with D_j ∼ D_j' − 4P₁ for the three generators D₁ = P₇ − P₉, D₂ = P₀ − 6P₁ + 2P₅ + P₇ + P₈ + P₉, D₃ = P₀ − 3P₁ + 2P₂ + P₄ + P₆ − P₇ − P₈ of G ∩ J(ℚ_5)¹ (Stoll p.10).
If D = [Q − P'] with Q in the disc of P' (Q₂ = ⋯ = Q_g = P'), the formula reduces to the tiny integral λ(t(Q)).

A degree-two closed point contributes Tr_{L/ℚ_p} λ(t(Q)), not one ℚ_p-rational point; a repeated point of multiplicity2 contributes 2λ(t(Q)). Reordering geometric conjugates leaves the effective divisor and value unchanged.

nodes.title: Coleman integrals of regular differentials are abelian integrals
nodes.statement: Let K be a finite extension of ℚ_p with residue field 𝔽_q, (𝒳, D) a good-reduction pair over O_K (ColemanIntegration:L1/good-reduction-pair) with generic fibre X of genus g ≥ 1, Y = 𝒳 − D, a ∈ ℂ_p a branch of the logarithm and (φ, ω•, M, g•) a Frobenius-structured datum on (𝒳, D) (L1/good-reduction-datum-exists). For every ω ∈ H⁰(X, Ω¹) ⊂ Ω⁺(Y) and all x, y ∈ ]Y_k[(ℂ_p), the Coleman integral of ColemanIntegration:L1/coleman-integral equals the abelian integral: ∫^{Col}_x^y ω = ∫_x^y ω = ⟨[y − x], ω_J⟩ (ED.4/abelian-integral over ℂ_p). Consequently the Coleman integral of a regular differential does not depend on the branch a or on the Frobenius lift, extends to all of X(ℂ_p), takes values in K' on points of X(K') for K' ⊆ ℂ_p finite over K, and vanishes on every degree-zero divisor whose class is torsion.
hypotheses: (𝒳, D) a good-reduction pair over O_K, K finite over ℚ_p; ω a regular differential on the proper curve X (not merely on Y).

The Frobenius-structured datum exists by ColemanIntegration:L1/good-reduction-datum-exists; its Frobenius matrix M has characteristic polynomial P_Y ∈ K[t] whose roots are Weil q-numbers of weights 1 and 2.
proofSteps: Let F be the Coleman primitive of ω with F(x) = 0 and η(P) := ⟨[P − x], ω_J⟩. On every residue disc of Y_k and on every end germ both are analytic primitives of ω: for F by L1/coleman-integral (f) and the vanishing of residues of the regular form ω; for η by ED.4/tiny-integral-expansion over finite extensions. Hence G := F − η is locally constant, an element of A_loc^a with dG = 0 (L1/locally-analytic-log-functions).

Cayley–Hamilton for M and φ*ω_i = Σ_j M_ij ω_j + dg_i give P_Y(φ*)ω = dh with h ∈ A⁺(Y); by L1/coleman-integral (a)–(c), P_Y(φ*)F − h is a Coleman function with zero differential, hence constant (L1/coleman-uniqueness-principle).

Let π be the q-power Frobenius endomorphism of J̃ = 𝒥_k, the Jacobian of the special fibre 𝒳_k, and P_J ∈ ℤ[t] its characteristic polynomial, so P_J(π) = 0 in End(J̃) (requested from DeligneWeightsAndPurity:DWP.1). Write P_J = Σ c_i t^i and fix x₀ ∈ ]Y_k[. For P in a wide open W on which φ is defined, Ψ(P) := Σ_i c_i [φ^i(P) − φ^i(x₀)] reduces to P_J(π)[P̃ − x̃₀] = 0, because φ reduces to the q-power Frobenius on points. Ψ is rigid analytic (ι algebraic, φ analytic, the group law of 𝒥 analytic) with values in the open polydisc of the kernel of reduction, so P ↦ ⟨Ψ(P), ω_J⟩ = log_F̂(s(Ψ(P)))·ω_J is analytic on W; thus P_J(φ*)η ∈ A⁺(Y) + ℂ_p (L1/wide-open-neighbourhood, ED.4/abelian-logarithm).

With Q := P_Y·P_J, Q(φ*)G lies in A⁺(Y) + ℂ_p and has zero differential, so it is constant (hypothesis (H0) of the datum). The roots of Q are Weil numbers of weights 1 and 2 (L1/good-reduction-datum-exists; DWP.1/weil-estimate-for-abelian-varieties), so none is a root of unity (L1/weil-weight-no-root-of-unity), and Dwork's principle (L1/dwork-principle (c)) shows that G is constant; G(x) = 0, so F = η.

Independence of a and of φ, rationality on K'-points and vanishing on torsion classes are now properties of η (ED.4/abelian-integral). This is the comparison of Katz–Rabinoff–Zureick-Brown Corollary 3.18 transported from Berkovich–Coleman integration to the Frobenius-continuation integral of ColemanIntegration L1.
acceptance: For y² = x⁶ + 8x⁵ + 22x⁴ + 22x³ + 5x² + 6x + 1 over ℚ_3 with D = closure of ∞⁺, the Coleman integral ∫^{Col}_{(0,1)}^{(−3,1)} dx/y equals the tiny integral ≡ 2·3 + 3⁴ (mod 3⁵) of ED.4/abelian-integral.
Degenerate case g = 1: for an elliptic curve with good reduction the Coleman integral of the invariant differential from O is the formal-group logarithm extended to E(ℂ_p).

nodes.title: Constants of integration on residue discs without a known rational point
nodes.statement: Let (X, O, p, 𝒳) be a good-reduction Chabauty datum, G ⊆ J(ℚ) a subgroup, ω ∈ H⁰(X_{ℚ_p}, Ω¹) with ⟨γ, ω_J⟩ = 0 for all γ ∈ G, η(P) := ∫_O^P ω, x̃ ∈ X̃(𝔽_p) and B ∈ D(x̃). Then η restricted to D(x̃) is η(B) + I_B(t) with I_B the tiny integral from B (ED.4/tiny-integral-expansion), and the constant η(B) can be certified by any of: (a) (Wetherell) if γ ∈ G satisfies red_J(γ) = red_J(ι_O(B)), then ι_O(B) − γ ∈ J¹(ℚ_p) and η(B) = ⟨ι_O(B) − γ, ω_J⟩, computed by ED.4/kernel-of-reduction-evaluation; (b) (torsion) if T ∈ J(ℚ_p) is torsion with red_J(T) = red_J(ι_O(B)) (for instance the unique such T of order prime to p when red_J(ι_O(B)) has order prime to p), then η(B) = ⟨ι_O(B) − T, ω_J⟩, again a kernel-of-reduction value; (c) (Coleman) η(B) = ∫^{Col}_O^B ω computed by Frobenius continuation on a good-reduction pair (𝒳, D) whose finite étale divisor D meets neither the residue disc of O nor D(x̃) (ED.4/coleman-abelian-comparison).
hypotheses: Good-reduction datum; ω annihilates G; B any ℚ_p-point of the disc (it exists since red is surjective).
proofSteps: η(B) = ⟨ι_O(B), ω_J⟩ (ED.4/abelian-integral (iii)); in (a) subtract ⟨γ, ω_J⟩ = 0, in (b) ⟨T, ω_J⟩ = 0 (torsion kernel); in both cases the difference reduces to 0 by red_J ∘ ι_O = ι_Õ ∘ red, so lies in J¹(ℚ_p) and its pairing is a sum of tiny integrals (ED.4/kernel-of-reduction-evaluation).

Existence of T in (b) for classes of order prime to p: the kernel J¹(ℚ_p) is a pro-p group, so the reduction map restricted to prime-to-p torsion is injective and Hensel's lemma for the étale group scheme 𝒥[n], p ∤ n, gives surjectivity onto J̃(𝔽_p)[n] (McCallum–Poonen Remark 8.3(1)).

(c) is ED.4/coleman-abelian-comparison for a good-reduction pair (𝒳, D) with O, B ∈ ]Y_k[: take for D the lift (Hensel's lemma, over the unramified extension of degree d) of a closed point of degree d of X̃ outside the residue classes of O and B.
Additivity η(P) = η(B) + ∫_B^P ω (ED.4/abelian-integral (i)) and the tiny-integral expansion give the form on D(x̃).
acceptance: For C₀(5) at p = 3 every residue disc contains a known rational point, so B can be taken rational and η(B) = 0; the theorem is needed only for discs without known points.
Degenerate case: if B ∈ X(ℚ) then γ = ι_O(B) ∈ J(ℚ) is allowed in (a) when G ⊇ ι_O(X(ℚ)) − ι_O(O), giving η(B) = 0.

nodes.title: The p-adic closure of a Mordell–Weil group: dimension at most the rank
nodes.statement: Let A be an abelian variety of dimension g over ℚ, p a prime, Γ ⊆ A(ℚ) ⊆ A(ℚ_p) a finitely generated subgroup of rank r and Γ̄ its closure in A(ℚ_p). Then (a) log_A(Γ̄) = ℤ_p·log_A(Γ) inside Lie(A_{ℚ_p}) ≅ ℚ_p^g; (b) the p-adic Lie subgroup Γ̄ has dimension r₀ := rank_{ℤ_p} ℤ_p·log_A(Γ) = dim_{ℚ_p} ℚ_p·log_A(Γ), and r₀ ≤ min(r, g); (c) if G ⊆ Γ has finite index then ℚ_p·log_A(G) = ℚ_p·log_A(Γ) and Ḡ has finite index in Γ̄; if moreover [Γ : G] is prime to p·#Ã(𝔽_p) for a prime p of good reduction, then Ḡ = Γ̄. Inequality r₀ < r can occur, and r₀ ≤ g always.
hypotheses: A abelian variety over ℚ (in ED.4, the Jacobian J of X); Γ finitely generated (Mordell–Weil theorem for Γ = J(ℚ), requested from HeightsRationalPointsAndObstructions:RP.1).

Closure is taken in the natural p-adic analytic topology on A(ℚ_p); the logarithm is the continuous geometric abelian logarithm, a local analytic isomorphism with finite torsion kernel. In the last clause A has good reduction and #Ã(𝔽_p) is the actual order of its reduced point group.
proofSteps: A(ℚ_p) is compact, so continuity of log gives log(Γ̄)=closure(log Γ). A finite generating family identifies ℤ_p log Γ as the continuous image of a compact finite product ℤ_p^r and hence a closed module; density of ℤ in ℤ_p gives the reverse inclusion. Finite generation is essential to this closed-image argument (McCallum–Poonen Lemma4.2 proof).
log_A is a local diffeomorphism (ED.4/abelian-logarithm (c)), so dim Γ̄ = rank of the ℤ_p-module ℤ_p log_A(Γ); it is at most rank_ℤ log_A(Γ) ≤ r and at most g.

For index n=[Γ:G], nΓ⊆G and Γ̄ is covered by finitely many translates of Ḡ, giving finite index and equal ℚ_p log spans. If gcd(n,p·#Ã(𝔽_p))=1, multiplication by n is a topological automorphism on the pro-p reduction kernel and on the finite reduction quotient. Its inverse preserves each closed subgroup: approximate n⁻¹ by integers simultaneously in the p-adic kernel and modulo the finite quotient order. Thus nΓ̄=Γ̄⊆Ḡ, and Ḡ=Γ̄ (Remark6.1).
acceptance: For C₀(5) (FPS Theorem 3, J(ℚ) ≅ ℤ) r = r₀ = 1 < g = 2 at every prime.
Degenerate case: Γ finite gives r₀ = 0 and Γ̄ = Γ.

nodes.title: Annihilating (vanishing) differentials of a Mordell–Weil subgroup
nodes.statement: Let X be a smooth projective geometrically integral curve of genus g ≥ 1 over ℚ with Jacobian J, p a prime, and Γ ⊆ J(ℚ_p) a subgroup. The space of differentials annihilating Γ is Ann_p(Γ) := {ω ∈ H⁰(X_{ℚ_p}, Ω¹) : ⟨γ, ω_J⟩ = 0 for all γ ∈ Γ} (pairing of ED.4/abelian-logarithm, ω_J as in ED.4/abelian-integral); under ω ↦ ω_J ∈ Module.Dual ℚ_p Lie(J_{ℚ_p}) it is the dual annihilator of the subspace ℚ_p·log_J(Γ). The annihilating (vanishing) differentials of X at p are Ann_p(J(ℚ)). For a good-reduction datum, the integral annihilator is V := Ann_p(Γ) ∩ H⁰(𝒳, Ω¹), a saturated ℤ_p-submodule, and Ṽ ⊆ H⁰(X̃, Ω¹) is its reduction mod p. Properties: (a) dim Ann_p(Γ) = g − r₀(Γ) ≥ g − rank Γ for Γ finitely generated (ED.4/padic-closure-dimension); (b) Ann_p(G) = Ann_p(Γ) when G ⊆ Γ has finite index, so Ann_p(J(ℚ)) is computed from generators D₁, …, D_r of any finite-index subgroup G of J(ℚ) (ED.3/finite-index-subgroup-certificate) as the kernel of the g × r matrix (∫_{D_j} ω_i) for a basis ω_i of H⁰; (c) Ann_p(Γ) = Ann_p(Γ̄) = Ann_p(Γ^sat), where Γ^sat = {x ∈ J(ℚ_p) : n x ∈ Γ for some n ≥ 1}; (d) Ann_p is inclusion-reversing; (e) dim_{𝔽_p} Ṽ = dim_{ℚ_p} Ann_p(Γ).
hypotheses: X/ℚ smooth projective geometrically integral of genus g; p prime; Γ a subgroup of J(ℚ_p), in applications the image of a finite-index subgroup of J(ℚ).
The integral lattice V and its reduction need a good-reduction datum; Ann_p itself does not.
proofSteps: Ann_p(Γ) is the preimage of Submodule.dualAnnihilator (span log Γ) under the isomorphism ω ↦ ω_J; finrank_add_finrank_dualAnnihilator gives (a) with r₀ = dim span.
(b): span log G = span log Γ by ED.4/padic-closure-dimension (c). (c): ⟨·, ω_J⟩ is continuous and ℚ_p is torsion-free. (d): Submodule.dualAnnihilator_anti.
(e): V is saturated in the free ℤ_p-module H⁰(𝒳, Ω¹) because Ann_p(Γ) is a ℚ_p-subspace, so V/pV injects into H⁰(X̃, Ω¹) and has dimension rank V = dim Ann_p(Γ) (Box §2.2.2).
acceptance: McCallum–Poonen (4): for C₀(5) at p = 3, Ann_3(J(ℚ)) = ℚ_3(ε dx/y + x dx/y), ε ≡ 2·3 + 3² + 2·3³ (mod 3⁴).
Stoll Lemma 5: for X₀^dyn(6) at p = 5 and G ≅ ℤ³, Ann_5(G) is one-dimensional with reduction ω̄₂ = w ω̄₀.

nodes.title: Certified p-adic precision of annihilating differentials
nodes.statement: Let (X, O, p, 𝒳) be a good-reduction Chabauty datum, ω₁, …, ω_g a ℤ_p-basis of H⁰(𝒳, Ω¹), D₁, …, D_r ∈ J(ℚ) with r < g, and M ∈ M_{g×r}(ℚ_p) the matrix M_{ij} = ∫_{D_j} ω_i, scaled by a power of p so that M has entries in ℤ_p. Suppose M' ∈ M_{g×r}(ℚ) has ℤ_(p)-entries with M − M' ∈ p^k M_{g×r}(ℤ_p), and that some r × r minor of M' on a row set R has valuation δ with 2δ < k. Then (a) M has rank r, the same minor of M has valuation δ, and dim Ann_p(⟨D₁, …, D_r⟩) = g − r; (b) for each i ∉ R the true annihilating differential ω^{(i)} := ω_i − Σ_{l ∈ R} x_l ω_l, where x ∈ ℚ_p^R solves Σ_{l∈R} x_l M_{l•} = M_{i•} (rows of M), satisfies x ∈ p^{−δ}ℤ_p^R and x − x' ∈ p^{k−2δ}ℤ_p^R for the solution x' of the same system with M'; (c) the ω^{(i)}, i ∉ R, form a basis of Ann_p(⟨D₁, …, D_r⟩), and p^δ ω^{(i)} is integral and known modulo p^{k−δ}. When ⟨D₁, …, D_r⟩ has finite index in J(ℚ) these are annihilating differentials of X with certified precision.
hypotheses: Good-reduction datum; the D_j generate a subgroup of rank r < g (certified by ED.3); entries of M are computed by ED.4/kernel-of-reduction-evaluation or tiny integrals to absolute precision p^k.
Valuations are certified by ED.0/valuation-certificate; p-adic approximations are those of ED.0/padic-embedding-certificate.
proofSteps: The minor of M differs from that of M' by an element of valuation ≥ k > δ, so it has valuation δ and M has rank r; (a) follows with ED.4/annihilating-differentials (a), (b).
Cramer's rule: M_R⁻¹ = adj(M_R)/det M_R has entries of valuation ≥ −δ; x' − x = M_R'⁻¹(m' − m) − M_R'⁻¹ E_R M_R⁻¹ m with E = M' − M, giving valuation ≥ k − 2δ.
The ω^{(i)} are linearly independent (each involves ω_i with coefficient 1) and annihilate the D_j by construction, so they span the (g − r)-dimensional annihilator.
acceptance: McCallum–Poonen Example 3: g = 2, r = 1, M = (∫ dx/y, ∫ x dx/y)ᵀ over [(−3,1) − (0,1)] known modulo 3⁵ with minor valuation δ = 1 on the row of dx/y; the theorem determines ε = −(∫ x dx/y)/(∫ dx/y) modulo 3^{5−2} = 3³, consistent with McCallum–Poonen's ε ≡ 2·3 + 3² + 2·3³ (mod 3⁴), which they obtain from the same data modulo 3⁵ because v(∫ x dx/y) = 2.
Degenerate case r = 0: M is empty, R = ∅ and every ω_i is annihilating, with no precision loss.

nodes.title: Zero bounds for integrals on a residue disc, including exceptional discs
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime and f = Σ_{i≥0} a_i t^i ∈ ℚ_p[[t]] with f' ∈ ℤ_p[[t]]. Then f converges on pℤ_p and f(pT) = Σ a_i p^i T^i has coefficients tending to 0. Use the extended valuation v(0) = +∞ throughout this node; in an implementation using Padic.valuation (which assigns 0 to zero), restrict minima to nonzero coefficients. Define the disc Strassmann index N_p(f) := the largest i with v(a_i) + i = min_j (v(a_j) + j), for f ≠ 0. (a) If f ≠ 0, f has at most N_p(f) zeros in pℤ_p. (b) (McCallum–Poonen Lemma 5.1) If m := ord_{t=0}(f' mod p) < p − 2, then N_p(f) ≤ m + 1. (c) (McCallum–Poonen Remark 5.2) If the coefficient of t^{p−1} in f' lies in pℤ_p and m < 2p − 2, then N_p(f) ≤ m + 1. (d) (certified index) If an index N and an integer μ satisfy a_N ≠ 0, v(a_N) + N = μ, and, for every i > N, either a_i = 0 or v(a_i) + i > μ, then f has at most N zeros in pℤ_p. Because v(a_i) ≥ −v_p(i) for i ≥ 1, the inequality for i > N holds automatically once i − v_p(i) > μ, so only finitely many indices need checking; if each coefficient a_i with i − v_p(i) ≤ μ is known modulo p^{k_i} with k_i + i > μ and the approximations satisfy both conditions, then the true coefficients satisfy them, and the bound holds for the true series. (e) Exceptional discs, m ≥ p − 2 or m unknown, are treated by (a) and (d): the bound is N_p(f) for the actual series, not m + 1. Applied to f = I_B on a residue disc (ED.4/tiny-integral-expansion, ED.4/disc-integration-constant), (a)–(e) bound the zeros of η on that disc.
hypotheses: p prime; f' ∈ ℤ_p[[t]] (scale ω so that it is integral with nonzero reduction); zeros counted as distinct points of pℤ_p.
In (d), 'known modulo p^{k_i}' means a certified rational approximation (ED.0/valuation-certificate).
proofSteps: (a) Apply Strassmann's theorem (ED.4/strassmann-bound, over ℚ_p) to g(T) = f(pT), whose coefficients a_i p^i tend to 0 because v(a_i) ≥ −v_p(i); the largest index of maximal |a_i p^i| is N_p(f); zeros t ∈ pℤ_p of f correspond to zeros T = t/p ∈ ℤ_p of g.

(b) v(a_{m+1}) = 0 and, for i > m + 1, v(a_i) ≥ −v_p(i) > m + 1 − i, because i − v_p(i) > m + 1 when m + 1 < p − 1; so the minimum of v(a_i) + i is attained at an index ≤ m + 1 (McCallum–Poonen Lemma 5.1 proof).

(c) The hypothesis excludes m = p − 1; for p ≤ i ≤ 2p − 1 only i = p has v_p(i) = 1, and there v(a_p) = v(w_{p−1}) − 1 ≥ 0; for i ≥ 2p one has i − v_p(i) > m + 1 (for p ≥ 3 because i − v_p(i) ≥ 2p − 1; for p = 2 the hypotheses force m = 0 and i − v_2(i) ≥ 2); so again no index beyond m + 1 is dominant.

nodes.title: Chabauty's theorem: finiteness when the closure of J(ℚ) is small
nodes.statement: Let X be a smooth projective geometrically integral curve of genus g ≥ 2 over ℚ with a rational point O, J its Jacobian, p a prime and r₀ the dimension of the p-adic closure of J(ℚ) in J(ℚ_p) (ED.4/padic-closure-dimension). If r₀ < g, in particular if r := rank J(ℚ) < g, then ι_O⁻¹(closure of J(ℚ)) ∩ X(ℚ_p) is finite; hence X(ℚ) is finite. Moreover, for p of good reduction its cardinality is at most Σ_{x̃ ∈ X̃(𝔽_p)} N_p(I_x̃) for any nonzero ω ∈ Ann_p(J(ℚ)) normalised to be integral with nonzero reduction, where I_x̃ is the expansion of η = ∫_O ω on D(x̃).
hypotheses: g ≥ 2; O ∈ X(ℚ); J(ℚ) finitely generated (Mordell–Weil, requested from RP.1).
For p of bad reduction the residue classes are those of the minimal regular model (ED.4/bad-reduction-bound).
proofSteps: Ann_p(J(ℚ)) has dimension g − r₀ ≥ 1 (ED.4/annihilating-differentials (a)); choose ω ≠ 0 in it, scaled to be integral with nonzero reduction.
η(P) = ⟨ι_O(P), ω_J⟩ is continuous and vanishes on J(ℚ), hence on its closure, so every point of ι_O⁻¹(closure) ∩ X(ℚ_p) is a zero of η.

For p of good reduction X(ℚ_p) is the union of the finitely many discs D(x̃) (ED.4/good-reduction-chabauty-datum); on each, η is η(B) + I_B(t) with I_B' = w ≠ 0 since ω ≠ 0 (ED.4/tiny-integral-expansion, ED.4/disc-integration-constant), so it has at most N_p zeros (ED.4/residue-disc-zero-bound (a)).
For an arbitrary p use the residue classes of the smooth locus of the minimal regular model, each parametrised by pℤ_p, with the same argument (ED.4/bad-reduction-bound).
X has good reduction at all but finitely many p, so X(ℚ) ⊆ ι_O⁻¹(J(ℚ)) ∩ X(ℚ_p) is finite whenever r < g.
acceptance: C₀(5) (rank 1, genus 2) and C₁(3₂) (rank 1, genus 2) have finitely many rational points; X₀^dyn(6) (genus 4) has finitely many rational points whenever rank J(ℚ) ≤ 3.
Sharpness of the hypothesis: when r₀ = g the closure of J(ℚ) is open in J(ℚ_p) and contains a neighbourhood of ι_O(O) in ι_O(X(ℚ_p)), so the closure set is infinite (McCallum–Poonen §7 (2)).

nodes.title: Coleman's effective Chabauty bound at a prime of good reduction
nodes.statement: Let (X, O, p, 𝒳) be a good-reduction Chabauty datum with g ≥ 2 and r₀ < g, and ω ∈ Ann_p(J(ℚ)) nonzero, scaled so that ω ∈ H⁰(𝒳, Ω¹) with nonzero reduction ω̃ ∈ H⁰(X̃, Ω¹). (a) For x̃ ∈ X̃(𝔽_p) with m := ord_x̃ ω̃, the number of P ∈ X(ℚ) with red P = x̃ is at most the number of zeros of η on D(x̃), hence at most N_p of the disc expansion, and at most m + 1 if m < p − 2. (b) If p > 2g, then #X(ℚ) ≤ #X̃(𝔽_p) + 2g − 2.
hypotheses: Good reduction at p; rank condition r₀ < g (in particular r < g); ω annihilates J(ℚ), which may be certified from any finite-index subgroup (ED.4/annihilating-differentials (b)).
proofSteps: (a) If D(x̃) contains Q ∈ X(ℚ), every P ∈ X(ℚ) ∩ D(x̃) satisfies ∫_Q^P ω = 0 because [P − Q] ∈ J(ℚ); by ED.4/tiny-integral-expansion this is a zero of I_Q(t(P)) with I_Q' = w and w mod p of order m at 0; apply ED.4/residue-disc-zero-bound (a), (b).

(b) Σ_{x̃ ∈ X̃(𝔽_p)} ord_x̃ ω̃ ≤ deg div(ω̃) = 2g − 2 (Riemann–Roch on X̃, requested from SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.3), so each m ≤ 2g − 2 < p − 2 when p > 2g, and summing (m_x̃ + 1) over X̃(𝔽_p) gives the bound (McCallum–Poonen Theorem 5.3 proof).
acceptance: McCallum–Poonen Example 1: y² = x(x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 5)(x − 6) at p = 7, rank 1, #X̃(𝔽_7) = 8, so #X(ℚ) ≤ 10, and the ten points (0,0), (1,0), (2,0), (5,0), (6,0), (3, ±6), (10, ±120), ∞ attain it.
Flynn–Poonen–Schaefer: for C₀(5) the best bound from (b) is 9 (p = 5), insufficient; the per-disc analysis at p = 3 (ED.4/fps-quintic-cycle-curve) gives 6.

nodes.title: Chabauty–Coleman at a prime of bad reduction via the minimal regular model
nodes.statement: Let X be a smooth projective geometrically integral curve of genus g ≥ 2 over ℚ with O ∈ X(ℚ), J its Jacobian with r₀ < g at the prime p, 𝒳 → Spec ℤ_p the minimal proper regular model of X_{ℚ_p} (StableReduction layer 5), 𝒳_s its special fibre, 𝒳^sm the smooth locus of 𝒳 → Spec ℤ_p and 𝒳_s^sm its special fibre. Residue classes are the fibres of red : X(ℚ_p) = 𝒳(ℤ_p) = 𝒳^sm(ℤ_p) → 𝒳_s^sm(𝔽_p); each class lies on a single component C of multiplicity 1 and is parametrised by pℤ_p through a local parameter. Let ω ∈ Ann_p(J(ℚ)) be nonzero. (1) For a multiplicity-one component C scale ω by a power of p so that its restriction ω̃_C to C^sm := C ∩ 𝒳^sm is a nonzero 1-form; for Q̃ ∈ C^sm(𝔽_p) with m := ord_Q̃ ω̃_C < p − 2, at most m + 1 points of X(ℚ) reduce to Q̃ (and at most N_p of the class expansion in general). (2) If n_C denotes the number of zeros of ω̃_C on C^sm(𝔽_p) counted with multiplicity, then Σ_{C of multiplicity 1} n_C ≤ 2g − 2. (3) If p > 2g, then #X(ℚ) ≤ #𝒳_s^sm(𝔽_p) + 2g − 2. (4) For every prime p with r₀ < g the set ι_O⁻¹(closure of J(ℚ)) ∩ X(ℚ_p) is finite.
hypotheses: Separately stated hypotheses: 𝒳 is the minimal proper regular model over ℤ_p (regularity is what makes X(ℚ_p) = 𝒳^sm(ℤ_p) and the intersection theory available); no smoothness of 𝒳 is assumed.
The scaling in (1) depends on C: ω_C = p^{k_C} ω with C absent from the divisor of ω_C as a section of the relative dualising sheaf.

The relative canonical sheaf ω_{𝒳/ℤ_p} of the local complete intersection 𝒳 → Spec ℤ_p, with ω_{𝒳/ℤ_p} ≅ Ω¹ on the smooth locus and compatibility with base change (Liu Proposition 6.4.9), is requested from SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.3.
proofSteps: Ω¹_{X/ℚ_p} ≅ ω_{𝒳/ℤ_p} ⊗ ℚ_p, so ω is a rational section of ω_{𝒳/ℤ_p} with canonical divisor K = H + V, H horizontal effective (ω regular on X) and V vertical (McCallum–Poonen Appendix A, p.13).

(1) Q̃ is a smooth point of 𝒳_s, so the residue-class parametrisation and tiny-integral expansion of ED.4/tiny-integral-expansion hold on its class (same proof, on the smooth locus); apply ED.4/residue-disc-zero-bound.

(2) Lemma A.3: (H.C)_P = ord_P(ω̃_C) for P ∈ C^sm, so n_C ≤ Σ_P (H.C)_P ≤ H.C. Lemma A.4: Σ_C n_C ≤ Σ_D m_D (H.D) = H.𝒳_s = K.𝒳_s = 2g − 2, using H.D ≥ 0, V.𝒳_s = 0 and the adjunction formula of StableReduction layer 5.
(3) Every rational point reduces into 𝒳_s^sm(𝔽_p), on a multiplicity-one component; sum (1) over classes and use (2) with m ≤ 2g − 2 < p − 2.
(4) Finitely many classes, each with finitely many zeros of η (ED.4/residue-disc-zero-bound (a)).
acceptance: Good reduction is the special case 𝒳 smooth, 𝒳_s = X̃ irreducible of multiplicity one, recovering ED.4/coleman-bound.

For X₀^dyn(6) at p = 2 the special fibre of the minimal regular model has five components A, B, C, C', D of multiplicity one (Stoll §2); (3) does not apply since p = 2 ≤ 2g, while (1) applies componentwise.

nodes.title: Integral differentials and residue-disc parameters for good-reduction hyperelliptic models
nodes.statement: Let p be an odd prime and f ∈ ℤ_p[x] squarefree of degree 2g + 1 or 2g + 2 (g ≥ 1) whose leading coefficient and discriminant are units of ℤ_p. Then the two affine charts y² = f(x) and v² = u^{2g+2} f(1/u), glued by x = 1/u, y = v/u^{g+1}, form a smooth projective model 𝒳 over ℤ_p of the hyperelliptic curve X : y² = f(x), and: (a) H⁰(𝒳, Ω¹) is free over ℤ_p with basis x^i dx/y, 0 ≤ i ≤ g − 1, reducing to the basis of H⁰(X̃, Ω¹) given by the same formulas; (b) local parameters: at an affine point (x₀, y₀) with ỹ₀ ≠ 0, t = x − x₀ with y = y₀√(f(x₀ + t)/y₀²) ∈ ℤ_p[[t]]; at a Weierstrass point (x̃₀, 0) of X̃, t = y, with x ∈ ℤ_p[[t]] determined by f(x) = t² and dx/y = 2 dt/f'(x); at a point at infinity (degree 2g + 2), t = u = 1/x, with x^i dx/y = −u^{g−1−i} du/v; at the point at infinity when deg f = 2g + 1 (the Weierstrass point u = v = 0), t = v, with u ∈ ℤ_p[[t]] determined by v² = u^{2g+2} f(1/u) and the same formula for x^i dx/y; (c) consequently ord_{∞^±}(x^i dx/y mod p) = g − 1 − i when deg f = 2g + 2, and ord_∞(x^i dx/y mod p) = 2(g − 1 − i) when deg f = 2g + 1, and for ω̃ = c(x) dx/y with c ∈ 𝔽_p[x] of degree ≤ g − 1 the order of ω̃ at an affine non-Weierstrass point x̃₀ is ord_{x̃₀}(c), and at a Weierstrass point x̃₀ it is 2·ord_{x̃₀}(c).
hypotheses: p odd; f has unit leading coefficient and unit discriminant (this gives good reduction of the displayed model); degree 2g + 1 or 2g + 2.
Shifted parameters t − t(Q) centred at a rational point Q of the disc are equally admissible.
proofSteps: Smoothness: the Jacobian criterion on both charts reduces to f̃ squarefree of degree 2g + 1 or 2g + 2 over 𝔽_p, p odd.

(a) Over the generic and the special fibre the forms x^i dx/y, i < g, are a basis of the regular differentials of a hyperelliptic curve (AlgebraicCurves layer 10, Stichtenoth Proposition 6.2.4); they are regular on 𝒳 and their reductions are independent, so they span the saturated lattice H⁰(𝒳, Ω¹).

(b) y is a unit on the disc of a non-Weierstrass point, so the binomial series gives the square root in ℤ_p[[t]]; at a Weierstrass point f'(x̃₀) ≠ 0 by squarefreeness, so x is a ℤ_p[[t]] solution of f(x) = t² by Hensel's lemma, and 2y dy = f'(x) dx; at infinity substitute x = 1/u.
(c) Read off orders from (b): x − x̃₀ has a double zero at a Weierstrass point in the parameter y.
acceptance: C₀(5) at p = 3: ω̃ = x dx/y has zeros of order 1 at (0, ±1) and order 0 at ∞^±; dx/y vanishes to order 1 at ∞^±.
C₁(3₂) at p = 3: (x − 1) dx/y has a double zero at the Weierstrass point (1, 0) and no other zeros, total 2 = 2g − 2.

nodes.title: Residue-disc verdicts: certified zero counts accounting for every zero
nodes.statement: For a genuine geometric Chabauty datum, a residue disc D(x̃), a certified nonzero differential annihilating a finite-index Mordell–Weil subgroup, and η(P)=∫_O^Pω, a ResidueDiscVerdict is finite raw data with a terminating checker, not a record containing a universal bound on unknown points. It contains: (i) exact curve/base-point/local-parameter identifiers and a certified integration constant; (ii) finite coefficient residue tables for scaled pullback series F(u)=p^sη(φ(p(a+p^k u))) in each encoded ball, where φ is the inverse geometric parameter chart and the finite integers a,k describe the ball (the root uses a=k=0), common absolute precision, a certified nonzero leading coefficient and a last dominant index; (iii) a finite tail-bound transcript whose soundness follows from integral differential coefficients or the CN.4 certified analytic supplier; (iv) either the whole disc as one leaf or a finite full residue-subdivision tree, with all p children at each internal ℤ_p-ball and disjoint leaves covering the root; (v) exact rational/algebraic zero records, their embeddings in ℚ_p via isolating balls, checks of the curve equation and geometric vanishing relation, rationality/nonrationality certificates and distinctness; (vi) for each leaf, the number of distinct recorded zeros equals its checked Strassmann upper bound. Zero-root leaves have bound0 and no point records. Valid means that every finite arithmetic, identifier, covering, disjointness and exact algebraic check succeeds. Under separately stated geometric interpretation and supplier-soundness hypotheses this proves X(ℚ)∩D(x̃)=Z_rat. No list of approximate roots, semantic all-point validity predicate or asserted bound is a raw certificate.
hypotheses: G of finite index in J(ℚ), so that ω also annihilates J(ℚ) (ED.4/annihilating-differentials (b)); without the finite-index certificate a verdict proves only that the rational points of D(x̃) whose image lies in the saturation of G are listed.
Distinct points of Z_rat ∪ Z_irr have distinct parameters t; points are compared exactly, not to finite precision.

Interpretation is external to the raw payload: a proved chart identifies every encoded ball with its geometric subdisc, the certified differential has integral derivative in the recorded coordinate, the integration constant and coefficient congruences are sound, and the imported tail producer certifies all omitted coefficients. These are theorems of the actual curve/integration and arithmetic suppliers, not arbitrary Prop fields stored in the certificate. The interpreted series on every rescaled closed unit disc is restricted (its coefficients tend to zero); a constant strict upper bound on the tail alone does not assert convergence.

Each nonrational zero is specified by exact algebraic coordinates/defining polynomials and a chosen ℚ_p embedding, with an exact nonrationality certificate. A Hensel-isolated analytic root alone does not prove rationality or nonrationality. Distinct zeros consume one unit of the distinct-zero bound; multiplicity is never inferred from rounded equality.

One sufficient root-disc tail rule is: for F(u)=p^s I(pu), s≥0, I′ integral and I≠0, v_p([u^n]F)≥s+n−v_p(n) for n≥1. If the chosen minimum coefficient valuation is m≥0, a cutoff K≥2(m+1) gives every n≥K valuation≥m+1. The constant coefficient is certified separately. The finite table modulo p^M must have M>m and must verify the last coefficient at valuation m. This rule is sufficient, not necessary; refinement may be needed.
proofSteps: Decode the finite input, check exact point equations and labels, normalize coefficient residues, replay the coefficient/tail arithmetic and every node of the finite subdivision tree. Check complete residue children rather than accepting a universal covering predicate. The checker returns false/undecided if its chosen precision does not isolate a dominant coefficient or support a strict tail bound.

Supplier soundness identifies each accepted finite coefficient table with the true pulled-back series modulo its stated precision and proves restrictedness and the strict infinite tail bound. The actual last dominant index is therefore at most the reported bound. Apply ED.4/strassmann-bound to the nonzero scaled series on the closed unit disc; nonzero scaling and chart substitution preserve its zeros.

Finite algebraic/group-relation certificates prove every listed point is a zero of η. Exact comparison or disjoint isolating balls establish distinctness. Equality of the number of listed distinct zeros and the checked upper bound proves exhaustion on each leaf.

The finite partition check gives exhaustive pairwise disjoint leaves. Every rational curve point in the root disc is a zero by the geometric annihilator and finite-index input, so it is one of the listed zeros; exact irrationality witnesses exclude Z_irr. Sum over leaves to conclude the rational-point equality.

Degenerate case: the empty verdict N = 0.
